title: The Price of an Inch
text:
In 2004 the management researchers Timothy Judge and Daniel Cable examined whether height matters at work. They first combined the results of dozens of earlier studies in a meta-analysis, and then analyzed four large surveys from the United States and Britain that had followed thousands of people through their working lives and recorded both their height and their earnings.

Taller people were consistently more successful. Height was linked to being seen as more of a leader, to being rated as more esteemed by others, to higher performance ratings and, above all, to higher pay. After accounting for sex, age and weight, each extra inch of height was associated with roughly 789 dollars more in yearly earnings in their estimates. Over a career, the difference between a short and a tall person added up to a large sum.

The authors argued that the link worked partly through how people see tall individuals and how tall people come to see themselves. Height seemed to raise self-esteem and social confidence, and others tended to treat taller people as more leaderlike and more authoritative. The effect was found for both men and women.
lesson: Physical presence quietly sways who gets chosen and paid more. When you evaluate or promote people, check that you are judging their work, not their stature.
location: USA and UK (meta-analysis and national surveys)
source: Judge, T. A., and Cable, D. M. (2004). The effect of physical height on workplace success and income: Preliminary test of a theoretical model. Journal of Applied Psychology, 89(3), 428-441.
caveat: The data are correlational, so the paper shows a reliable link rather than proof that height itself causes the advantage.
